newsitem.title: THAILAND: Rumours batter Thai stocks, hurt baht.
newsitem.headline: Rumours batter Thai stocks, hurt baht.

text.p: Market rumours that some brokerages may be hit by client defaults on margin loans battered Thai stocks on Friday, while offshore speculation of a possible devaluation depressed the baht, dealers said.
The index, after falling heavily on Thursday, continued its slide in Friday morning trade, crashing through the psychologically important 1,000-point level to a 35-month low.
Dealers said forced selling by brokers of stocks held by investors unable to maintain funds in their accounts was behind much of the recent falls.
The SET Index was down 2.26 percent, or 23.13 points, to 999.55 as the market closed for lunch.
The Index has fallen 79.64 points, or 7.4 percent, this week to Thursday's close.
The baht fell to 25.340-25.345 against the U.S. dollar at midday from 25.334-25.337 in early morning trade on heavy buying of the American currency against the baht by offshore players, dealers said.

They said the baht was hit by the devaluation rumours started by some Singapore investors. The rumours, which were rife in July, resurfaced because some of them expected the baht to be devalued to help Thailand boost sagging exports.
The Thai central bank denied the rumour.
"I just received a report about the rumour in Singapore. I want to stress that baht devaluation is not in any way planned by the bank," Bank of Thailand spokeswoman Kleo-thong Hetrakul told Reuters.

Dealers in Singapore said Thailand's looming political crisis, with an opposition no-confidence motion against Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa set for parliamentary debate on September 18, provided fodder for attacks on Thai markets.
The markets also took a beating because of the U.S. missile attacks on Iraq, higher oil prices and the downgrading of Thailand's short-term ratings by Moody's Investors Service, they said.
Market analysts said they expected the stock and money markets to remain depressed as there was no sign the forced selling of stocks would stop immediately.
The negative mood was expected to prevail despite a statement by the Thai stock exchange on Thursday that there were no brokerages with financial problems or client defaults.

"Right now, there is no positive news and there are no chances for the (stock) index to rebound," said one broker. "The market fundamentals are now changed after the index fell below the psychologically important 1,000 points."
Said a broker at First Asia Securities: "local investors are being forced to sell shares as they didn't have enough money to pay for margin loans."
Two Thai brokerages, Sitca Finance and Securities Plc and First City Investments Plc, said on Friday that their financial positions were stable in the face of the market rumours.
On the baht, some analysts said the rumours generated from Singapore were unfounded because the currency was reasonably stable in the Thai market.
"These are all self-serving rumours from Singapore. I know. used to work there," said the treasury manager of a foreign bank.

"There was heavy baht selling for the dollar near lunch break by players in Singapore," said a senior dealer at a local bank. "They usually attack the baht during the lunch break here and after the Bank of Thailand's dollar market operation with domestic commercial banks is closed."
